draft.title: Bounded willpower
card: Bounded willpower means people often know what is best for them in the long run but do not act on it. Their self-control is limited.
Many people choose a smaller reward now over a larger reward later. This is called favouring the present.
Common examples are spending money instead of saving it, skipping exercise, or putting off study until the night before a test.
Traditional economics assumes people stick to plans that serve them best. Bounded willpower shows that people may fail to do so, even when they want to.
draft.remember: Bounded willpower: people can know what is best later but still pick what feels good now.

a.q: Jack in Ballarat wants to save for a car. He gets paid on Friday and spends most of it on a new gaming headset. Which idea does this best show?
opts: A lack of any wish to save
a.why: Jack wants the car, which is a later goal, but gives in to a purchase that feels good now. That is limited self-control. It is not a lack of wish to save, because he does have the goal.
a.clue: He has a goal but does not follow it.

b.q: Priya in Geelong signs up for a gym with a yearly plan because she wants to be fit. After two weeks she stops going, and she says she will start again next month. Why does this show bounded willpower?
opts: She wants long-run fitness but acts on what is easier now
She is too short of information about gyms to choose well
She cares more about the gym owner than about herself
She is comparing costs and benefits to get the best result
b.why: Priya states a long-run aim but chooses the easier option in the present. That gap between her plan and her action is bounded willpower. Lack of information would be a different idea, and she knew what the plan involved.
b.clue: Look for the gap between her goal and what she does.

b.best: She wants long-run fitness but acts on what is easier now
